trap: Becomes a self-help parable ("keep your eyes on Jesus, not the waves") or a shame-story about Peter's "little faith" — missing that Jesus comes walking toward them in the storm before Peter asks anything, and catches him the instant he calls.
hinge: He rebukes Peter's "little faith" — but it was a little faith that got him out of the boat and walking on water in the first place, more than the other eleven managed.

doors.claim: Jesus walks toward the disciples in their fourth-watch panic before any of them asks for help — the initiative is his, not Peter's daring.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: The Lord came to visit His disciples who are tossed on the sea in the fourth watch of the night — that is, at its close.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: Christ then did not reveal Himself to His disciples until they cried out; for the more intense their fear, the more did they rejoice in His presence.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Sometimes the Church is so afflicted that she seems utterly forsaken by God: but God does not forsake her. Though not present, and though he defers, yet he sees and strengthens.

doors.say: He was already walking toward the boat before anyone in it knew to hope for him.
doors.do: Ask them to name the storm they assume they're facing alone, and name whose feet are already on the water.

doors.claim: Peter's faith is real even though it falters — he asks to do the very thing Christ is doing, and is answered.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: See how great his warmth, how great his faith. He said not, Pray and entreat for me; but 'Bid me.'

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: This I am not able by myself, but in Thee I am able. Peter confessed what he was in himself, and what he should receive from Him.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: If it be thou — it is the same as, Since it is thou. St. Peter was in no doubt, or he would not have quitted the ship.

doors.say: Peter didn't ask Jesus to calm the sea for him — he asked to walk on it with him. That is faith, not presumption.
doors.do: Have them name one impossible thing they've stopped asking for because it seemed presumptuous, and ask again.

doors.claim: The sinking is not the end of the story — Christ's hand is faster than Peter's fear.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: He bade not the winds to cease, but stretched forth His hand and caught him, because his faith was required.

witnesses.author: Rabanus Maurus
witnesses.reading: The Lord looked back upon him, and brought him to repentance; He stretched forth His hand, and forgave him, and thus the disciple found salvation.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: He is left a little to temptation, that faith may be increased; for as he believed that by his command he could be upheld upon the waves, so, while he sinks, that he could be saved by his power.

doors.say: He did not still the wind first — he caught Peter first. The rescue came before the calm.
doors.do: Ask them to recall a moment they were caught mid-fall, and name whose hand it was.

doors.claim: God does not come in the wind, the quake, or the fire, but after them, in a voice quiet enough to be missed.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: A still voice — to intimate, that God would do his work in and for Israel in his own time, not by might or power, but by his own spirit, which moves with a powerful, but yet with a sweet and gentle gale.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Think not that the Lord comes with the wind, but after the wind of commotion; fire shall pass by, then a whistling of a thin air, after this the Lord shall pass by, that he may speak with thee.

doors.say: Elijah wanted fire from heaven again. God came as a whisper, and the whisper was enough.
doors.do: Ask them to take ten minutes of real quiet this week and listen, before asking God for anything louder.

doors.claim: Elijah's despair rests on a mistake: he is not alone, and part of his healing is being told about the seven thousand.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: I have left — or, I have reserved to myself; I have kept from the common contagion: therefore thou art mistaken to think that thou art left alone.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: What was hard for so great a prophet to know, that servants had remained to God in this world? He enlightens himself with a ray of humility who subtly weighs the good things of others.

doors.say: Elijah was sure he was the last faithful person in Israel. He was wrong by seven thousand.
doors.do: Have them name someone else still faithful in the place they feel most alone, and reach out to that person this week.

complementary.gravity: Elijah, spent and hiding in a cave, is sure he alone is left, and God passes by not in the wind, the earthquake, or the fire but in a still small voice (1 Kings 19); the Psalm resolves to listen for what the Lord will speak; Paul says the word is near, in your mouth and in your heart (Romans 10); and Jesus comes across the water to frightened men and says, "It is I; be not afraid." The nerve: God meets fear and exhaustion not with spectacle but with a near and quiet word.

synthesis.convergence: Elijah hears God not in the storm but in a still voice (1 Kings 19); the psalmist waits for a word of peace (Psalm 85); Paul insists the word is near, on your lips and in your heart (Romans 10); and over the waves Jesus speaks to the frightened: "It is I" (Matthew 14). Each reading brings God close in a voice rather than a display, to people who thought they had been left alone in the storm.
synthesis.claim: When you are sure you are alone and the storm is loudest, God comes near in a quiet word: it is I, do not be afraid.
synthesis.here: For people worn out by crisis and braced for the next loud thing, the move is not more effort but quieter attention, and the news that they are not the only faithful one left.

semicontinuous.gravity: Joseph is sold into a pit by his own brothers in the wilderness (Genesis 37); the Psalm recalls how God led Joseph, "bound in fetters," until the appointed word came to pass (Psalm 105); Paul insists faith comes only by a word that must first be sent and heard (Romans 10); and Peter steps out onto the sea and sinks the moment he looks at the wind. The nerve: faith is tested exactly in the gap between the word that calls and the ground giving way beneath it.

synthesis.convergence: Joseph is dragged into a storm not of his making, and God is present in the pit before Joseph can see it (Genesis 37; Psalm 105); Paul insists faith comes only by a word that must first be sent and heard (Romans 10); Peter steps onto chaos and does not drown because a hand is already reaching. Every reading agrees: God is present in the crisis before you can name it, calling by a word that precedes your faith.
synthesis.claim: The storm did not start when you noticed it — Christ was already walking toward you across it.
synthesis.here: For people paralyzed by "not enough faith," don't demand more faith — point at whose hand is already extended. Their little faith is what got them out of the boat, and it is enough to be caught.

subtract: Three landings — Christ's initiative, Peter's daring ask, or the catching hand. Choose one and let the others go.
source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain), Wesley's Explanatory Notes, and the Glossa ordinaria (Migne recension, Wroot Press English), retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
